title: The Experimenter’s Mindset: What Children’s Natural Curiosity Can Teach Schools About AI
author: Andrew Marcinek
summary: Marcinek uses his two-year-old daughter's relentless experimenting, and Alison Gopnik's research on children as scientists, to argue that schools should introduce AI to teachers the way children meet anything new: with permission to explore. He sets this against evidence of teacher burnout and unsupported change, including RAND, Pew, OECD and Auburn findings that new platforms piled on top of old obligations raise burnout. His claim is that top-down mandates to adopt AI by next quarter produce resistance or box-ticking, while districts that began by addressing teacher fear did better. He offers a concrete adoption path: unstructured exploration time, naming discomfort, teacher-chosen small experiments, shared stories of what flopped, and removing something from teachers' plates. The culture of the school must match the message, or a call to experiment becomes another mandate.
points: Young children learn by testing hypotheses, and adults adopting AI need the same permission and safety to explore before they are expected to be expert.
Teacher stress tracks constant unsupported change more than resource shortages, so adding AI without removing obligations deepens burnout.
RAND found the most effective early AI training addressed teachers' fear and discomfort rather than jumping into instructional applications.
Low current AI use among teachers is read as a field in its early exploration phase, not a failure.
A school that says experiment but punishes missteps is not supporting experimentation, so culture has to match the message.
quotes: The difference is that we give toddlers permission to experiment. We expect the mess. We know it’s how they learn. But when it comes to teachers and AI, we often skip straight to expectations and outcomes without leaving room for the exploration that has to come first.
That’s not an indictment of teachers. It’s an indictment of a system that has piled so much onto educators’ plates that curiosity becomes a luxury rather than a priority.

A 2024 Auburn University study put a finer point on this. When schools introduced new learning management systems without removing old requirements, teachers reported higher burnout. The platforms weren’t replacing existing work—they were piling on top of it.
This is the opposite of how most schools approach new technology. The typical model is top-down: here’s the tool, here’s the training, start using it by next quarter.
Those numbers don’t represent failure. They represent a field still in the early exploration phase. And that’s exactly where it should be.
A school that says “experiment with AI” but punishes missteps or demands immediate results isn’t actually supporting experimentation. The culture has to match the message.

AI doesn’t need to be conquered overnight. It doesn’t need to be feared. It needs to be explored—at a human pace, with human judgment, and with the same spirit of curiosity that we hope to cultivate in our students.
